## Subsection B: Program Design & Activities (~1,050 words / 2 pages)

**Theory of Change**

Family Literacy Pathways is built on a well-established premise: when parents gain literacy and educational credentials, the benefits extend directly to their children. Adults who complete GED programs demonstrate higher rates of employment and economic stability, and research consistently shows that parental literacy is one of the strongest predictors of early childhood reading success (Mol & Bus, 2011; National Institute for Literacy, 2020). ReadForward Community Literacy has operationalized this two-generation logic into three integrated program components delivered over 18 months: adult literacy and GED preparation, parent-child shared reading, and employment readiness coaching. Each component addresses a distinct barrier identified in the community needs assessment, and together they create a reinforcing cycle — as parents gain skills and confidence, they engage more actively with their children's learning, which in turn deepens their own motivation to persist.

**Program Components**

*Component 1: Adult Literacy and GED Preparation.* The core of Family Literacy Pathways is a structured, instructor-led literacy curriculum delivered in two cohorts of 75 participants each across the 18-month grant period. Classes meet three times per week, two hours per session, at [Partner Site — e.g., Eastside Community Center] in zip codes 12345 and 12346, eliminating transportation as a barrier for participants in our highest-need areas. Instruction follows the Evidence-Based Adult Education framework, contextualized to real-life tasks — reading utility bills, filling out job applications, interpreting school communications — to maximize engagement and relevance for low-income parents. Each participant receives an individualized learning plan developed at intake by a credentialed adult education instructor, with progress reviewed every eight weeks. GED preparation is introduced at the intermediate level and accelerated for participants who reach benchmark literacy scores, ensuring the most ready learners move toward credentialing within the grant period.

*Component 2: Parent-Child Shared Reading.* Twice monthly, participants attend a 90-minute Family Reading Night, offered in coordination with the Eastside County Public Library. Each session is facilitated by a literacy coach and pairs adult learners with their K–3 children for structured read-aloud activities, followed by brief parent coaching on at-home reading strategies. This component directly addresses the district's finding that 1,200 K–3 students are reading below grade level, recognizing that classroom instruction alone is insufficient without reinforcement at home. Participants receive a take-home book bag at enrollment and replenish their libraries at each Family Reading Night, removing cost as a barrier to daily reading practice.

*Component 3: Employment Readiness Coaching.* In months 10–18, participants who have reached intermediate literacy benchmarks transition into a six-session employment readiness workshop series, covering résumé writing, interview skills, workplace communication, and financial literacy basics. Sessions are delivered in partnership with the Eastside County Workforce Board, which has pledged $20,000 toward this component and will provide direct connections to job placement services for participants who complete GED preparation. This sequencing is intentional: employment content is introduced after participants have built sufficient literacy skills to engage with written materials and self-advocacy tasks, increasing the likelihood that coaching translates into actual job attainment.

**Participant Pathway**

All participants enter through a standardized intake process that includes a literacy assessment (TABE 11/12), goal-setting interview, and eligibility verification. ReadForward's current waitlist of 78 adults will be prioritized for Cohort 1 enrollment, ensuring immediate impact from grant launch. Participants who miss three consecutive sessions are contacted by the program coordinator for a retention check-in; those facing acute barriers (childcare, transportation, work schedule conflicts) are connected to wraparound supports through partner referrals. At program exit, each participant receives a transition plan outlining next steps — GED testing, job placement services, or enrollment in postsecondary education — with a 90-day follow-up contact to track outcomes.

## Subsection C: Outcomes & Evaluation (~530 words / 1 page)

**Measurable Outcomes and Objectives**

Family Literacy Pathways will achieve the following outcomes across 150 adult learners over 18 months. Outputs and outcomes are distinguished clearly to allow precise tracking of both service delivery and participant change.

*Output 1:* 150 adult learners enrolled in Family Literacy Pathways across two cohorts.

*Outcome 1 — Literacy Gains:* By month 18, 80% of participants who complete at least 60% of scheduled instruction (a minimum of 108 contact hours) will demonstrate measurable literacy gains of at least one TABE grade-level equivalent, as measured by pre/post TABE 11/12 assessment. Baseline: intake TABE scores, collected at enrollment.

*Outcome 2 — GED Attainment:* By month 18, 40 participants (27% of total enrolled) will have passed one or more GED subject-area tests, and 25 will have earned their GED credential. Baseline: zero participants currently hold a GED credential at enrollment (verified at intake).

*Outcome 3 — Parent-Child Reading Frequency:* By month 18, 70% of participants attending at least six Family Reading Nights will report reading aloud with their child three or more times per week, up from a self-reported baseline of 28% at intake (ReadForward intake survey, 2024).

*Outcome 4 — Employment Readiness:* By month 18, 60% of participants completing the employment readiness workshop series will demonstrate proficiency on a standardized workplace readiness rubric, and 30 participants will have obtained employment or enrolled in postsecondary education within 90 days of program exit.

**Evaluation Design and Methods**

ReadForward will use a pre/post design with three measurement points — intake, mid-program (month 9), and exit — to track individual participant progress against each outcome. The evaluation draws on four data streams:

The TABE 11/12, a nationally normed and widely used adult literacy assessment, will measure literacy gains at all three points. Attendance and participation records, maintained in ReadForward's existing database, will track dosage and flag retention risks in real time. A participant self-report survey, administered at intake and exit, will capture reading frequency with children, employment status, and self-efficacy. At 90 days post-exit, the program coordinator will conduct structured follow-up contacts to document credential attainment, employment, and postsecondary enrollment.

The Lead Adult Education Instructor will be responsible for assessment administration and data integrity. The Program Director will compile and analyze data quarterly, producing brief internal reports that identify underperforming activities and inform mid-course adjustments. For example, if mid-program TABE scores show a cohort is not on track for the literacy-gain outcome, the Director and Lead Instructor will review pacing and individualized learning plans within two weeks of the data review.

**Learning and Improvement**

Evaluation findings will be shared with ReadForward's board of directors annually and with the Bright Futures Foundation in quarterly progress reports. At program close, ReadForward will produce a final evaluation summary documenting outcomes against targets, lessons learned, and recommendations for program replication or scale — contributing to the broader field of two-generation literacy practice.

## Subsection D: Budget & Budget Narrative (~480 words / 1 page)

**Budget Summary**

ReadForward Community Literacy requests $150,000 from the Bright Futures Foundation to support 18 months of Family Literacy Pathways. An additional $45,000 in leveraged resources — $25,000 in in-kind facility space and $20,000 in cash from the Eastside County Workforce Board — brings the total program investment to $195,000, reducing the cost to this funder to $1,000 per participant served.

**Personnel ($124,500 / 63.8% of request)**

Personnel costs fund five positions totaling 3.25 FTE, each essential to program delivery. The Program Director (0.5 FTE, $30,000) provides oversight, manages funder reporting, and coordinates partner relationships — a half-time allocation appropriate given ReadForward's existing infrastructure. The Lead Adult Education Instructor (1.0 FTE, $45,000) delivers all core literacy instruction and GED preparation, the highest-cost position reflecting the credential and full-time commitment required. The Literacy Coach (0.75 FTE, $22,500) facilitates Family Reading Nights and provides participant retention support, with a three-quarter allocation matched to the twice-monthly session schedule and ongoing coaching load. The Employment Readiness Coordinator (0.5 FTE, $15,000) leads the six-session workshop series and maintains the Workforce Board partnership; this position is funded jointly with the Workforce Board's $20,000 cash contribution, making it effectively cost-neutral to this grant. The Program Coordinator (0.5 FTE, $12,000) manages intake, data entry, scheduling, and childcare stipend disbursement.

**Fringe Benefits ($25,500 / 20% of personnel)**

Fringe is calculated at 20% of personnel costs, covering FICA, health insurance contributions, and workers' compensation. This rate is consistent with ReadForward's current fringe rate as reflected in our 2023 audit.

**Program Supplies and Books ($6,000)**

Supplies fund take-home book bags, reading materials for Family Reading Nights, and GED preparation workbooks for 150 participants. Per-participant cost is $40, a modest investment that removes a direct financial barrier to engagement and extends learning beyond classroom hours.

**Childcare Stipends and Transportation ($8,000)**

This line funds per-session childcare stipends and transportation assistance for participants who would otherwise be unable to attend consistently. These supports address the two barriers most frequently cited in ReadForward's exit surveys from prior cohorts. Stipends are disbursed by the Program Coordinator upon verified attendance, ensuring accountability.

**Facility Rental and Utilities ($3,000)**

ReadForward has negotiated a discounted rate with its facility partner. The in-kind contribution of $25,000 — the difference between market-rate rental and the discounted cost — is reflected in the leveraged funds column of the budget table.

**Evaluation and Data Systems ($6,000)**

This line covers TABE 11/12 assessment materials, database licensing, and costs associated with the 90-day follow-up protocol. Robust evaluation is a program priority, not an afterthought; this allocation ensures data quality sufficient to support learning and future replication.

**Indirect Costs ($12,000 / 8%)**

Indirect costs are calculated at 8% of direct costs, below the federal de minimis rate of 10%, reflecting ReadForward's commitment to directing the maximum share of grant funds to direct services.

**Cost Effectiveness**

At $1,000 per participant — or $6,000 per GED credential earned, assuming 25 completers — Family Literacy Pathways compares favorably to the national average cost of $7,200–$9,000 per GED completer in community-based programs (American Institutes for Research, 2022). The $45,000 in leveraged resources represents a 30-cent local match for every dollar requested, demonstrating community investment and reducing financial risk to the Bright Futures Foundation.

## Subsection E: Organizational Capacity & Sustainability (~475 words / 1 page)

**Organizational Track Record**

ReadForward Community Literacy has operated in Eastside County for 12 years with a singular focus: expanding literacy access for low-income adults and families. Since our founding, we have served more than 2,400 adult learners across our core programs, maintaining consistent outcomes that position Family Literacy Pathways as a natural extension of proven work rather than an untested initiative. In our most recent program year, 76% of active participants demonstrated at least one TABE grade-level gain, and 18 participants earned their GED credential — results achieved without the structured two-generation design and dedicated employment pathway that this grant would fund.

ReadForward currently manages two active grants totaling $210,000 annually, demonstrating our capacity to administer funding of comparable scale to this request. Our 2023 independent audit returned clean financials with no findings, and we maintain six months of operating reserves — a level of fiscal stability that insulates program participants from disruption if grant timelines shift.

**Partnerships**

Family Literacy Pathways rests on three formalized partnerships. The Eastside County Public Library hosts and co-facilitates Family Reading Nights, contributing staff time and library card enrollment for all participants; this relationship has been active for four years. The Eastside County Workforce Board has committed $20,000 in cash support for the employment readiness component and will provide direct referrals to job placement services for program completers; a memorandum of understanding formalizing this commitment is included in the attachments. Eastside County Community College has agreed to serve as a referral destination for participants pursuing postsecondary education after GED attainment, with a designated advisor assigned to ReadForward referrals — a pathway that meaningfully extends program impact beyond the grant period.

**Leadership and Staff Capacity**

ReadForward's Program Director brings 14 years of adult education experience and has managed federal and foundation grants at this scale previously. The Lead Adult Education Instructor position will be filled by an internal candidate currently serving as an adjunct instructor in our existing program, reducing onboarding time and ensuring continuity of instructional quality from day one. All key personnel resumes are included in the attachments.

**Sustainability Plan**

ReadForward is committed to sustaining Family Literacy Pathways beyond the 18-month grant period. Our sustainability strategy rests on three pillars. First, the Eastside County Workforce Board has indicated willingness to expand its cash commitment in Year 2, contingent on employment outcome data from this grant — an outcome ReadForward is confident in achieving given our evaluation design. Second, we are preparing an application to the state adult education formula grant program (WIOA Title II), for which Family Literacy Pathways' two-generation design makes us a strong candidate; that application will be submitted in the fall of Year 1. Third, ReadForward's individual donor program, which currently generates $18,000 annually, is targeted to grow to $30,000 by Year 2 through a planned major gifts campaign. Together, these sources are projected to cover 80–90% of program costs in Year 2, with a gap-funding strategy in place should any single source fall short.

# PROJECT SUMMARY
*(300 words max — target: 290 words)*

ReadForward Community Literacy requests $150,000 from the Bright Futures Foundation to deliver Family Literacy Pathways, an 18-month two-generation literacy and workforce program serving 150 low-income adults in Eastside County (zip codes 12345 and 12346) from July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027.

Eastside County faces a literacy crisis with direct consequences for children and families. Twenty-two percent of Eastside adults lack a high school diploma, nearly double the statewide rate of 11% (ACS, 2022), and the local school district reports 1,200 K–3 students reading below grade level (District Literacy Report, 2023). Yet 78 adults are currently on ReadForward's waitlist for literacy classes, with no comparable two-generation program available in the county.

Family Literacy Pathways addresses this need through three integrated components: structured adult literacy instruction and GED preparation (three sessions per week), twice-monthly parent-child Family Reading Nights, and a six-session employment readiness workshop series introduced at month ten. Grounded in evidence-based adult education practice, the program moves participants from intake assessment through individualized literacy instruction, family engagement, and workforce preparation, with childcare stipends and transportation assistance ensuring equitable access throughout. A dedicated team of 3.25 FTE staff, supported by partnerships with the Eastside County Public Library and the Eastside County Workforce Board, will deliver all program components.

By December 31, 2027, Family Literacy Pathways will achieve the following: 80% of active participants will demonstrate at least one TABE grade-level literacy gain; 25 participants will earn their GED credential; 70% of Family Reading Night participants will report reading aloud with their child three or more times per week; and 30 participants will obtain employment or enroll in postsecondary education within 90 days of exit.

At $1,000 per participant, this program represents a sound investment. ReadForward contributes $45,000 in leveraged resources and brings 12 years of demonstrated adult literacy experience to this work.

## A. Need & Community Impact
*(1 page — target: 550 words)*

**The Problem**

Adult learners in Eastside County face educational disadvantage at rates that far exceed state and national benchmarks. According to the American Community Survey (2022), 22% of Eastside adults lack a high school diploma, compared with 11% statewide — a gap that has persisted and widened over the past decade as the local economy has shifted toward jobs requiring basic credentialing. The consequences extend beyond individual adults: the Eastside County School District reports that 1,200 K–3 students are currently reading below grade level (District Literacy Report, 2023), a figure that correlates directly with the county's high rate of parental educational attainment. Research consistently links low parental literacy to reduced at-home reading frequency, lower early childhood school readiness, and diminished long-term academic outcomes for children — making adult literacy a family-level and community-level crisis, not an individual one.

**Who Is Most Affected**

The burden falls most heavily on low-income parents in Eastside County's highest-need zip codes, 12345 and 12346, where poverty rates are significantly above the county average and access to educational programming is most limited. ReadForward's service area within these zip codes is home to an estimated 4,200 adults who lack a high school diploma, the majority of whom are parents of school-age children. Adults in this population face compounding barriers: limited transportation, inflexible work schedules, childcare responsibilities, and in many cases prior negative experiences with formal education that have eroded confidence and motivation. These are not obstacles that standard adult education programs — typically daytime, center-based, and without family supports — are designed to address.

**Gaps in Existing Services**

Eastside County has limited adult education infrastructure. The only other provider of adult literacy services in the county serves approximately 90 participants annually through a single daytime program, leaving the vast majority of the estimated need unmet. No program in the county combines adult literacy instruction with family literacy components and employment readiness support in an integrated model — the combination that research identifies as most effective for low-income parents (National Institute for Literacy, 2020). The scale of unmet need is visible in ReadForward's own data: as of the date of this application, 78 adults are on our waitlist for literacy classes, with an average wait of four months before a seat becomes available.

**Community Voice**

The community has named this need directly. In ReadForward's 2024 intake survey (n=94), 81% of respondents identified reading and literacy skills as their most significant personal barrier to employment, and 67% reported that they rarely or never read aloud with their children at home — not because they did not want to, but because they felt their own reading skills were insufficient. These findings shaped every element of Family Literacy Pathways' design, from the integration of family reading into the program model to the provision of childcare stipends that make consistent attendance possible. The Eastside County Workforce Board and the Eastside County Public Library, both formal partners in this initiative, have affirmed the depth of this need through their own client and patron data and have committed resources accordingly.

The need in Eastside County is clear, well-documented, and unmet. Family Literacy Pathways is designed to respond directly — with a two-generation model, a defined target population, and an evidence-based approach that addresses both the immediate skills gap and its long-term consequences for children and families.

## B. Program Design & Activities
*(2 pages — target: 1,075 words)*

**Theory of Change**

Family Literacy Pathways is built on a well-established premise: when parents gain literacy and educational credentials, the benefits extend directly to their children. Adults who complete GED programs demonstrate higher rates of employment and economic stability, and research consistently shows that parental literacy is one of the strongest predictors of early childhood reading success (Mol & Bus, 2011; National Institute for Literacy, 2020). ReadForward Community Literacy has operationalized this two-generation logic into three integrated program components delivered over 18 months: adult literacy and GED preparation, parent-child shared reading, and employment readiness coaching. Each component addresses a distinct barrier identified in the community needs assessment, and together they create a reinforcing cycle — as parents gain skills and confidence, they engage more actively with their children's learning, which in turn deepens their own motivation to persist.

**Program Components**

*Component 1: Adult Literacy and GED Preparation.* The core of Family Literacy Pathways is a structured, instructor-led literacy curriculum delivered in two cohorts of 75 participants each across the 18-month grant period. Classes meet three times per week, two hours per session, at Eastside Community Center in zip codes 12345 and 12346, eliminating transportation as a barrier for participants in our highest-need areas. Instruction follows the Evidence-Based Adult Education framework, contextualized to real-life tasks — reading utility bills, filling out job applications, interpreting school communications — to maximize engagement and relevance for low-income parents. Each participant receives an individualized learning plan developed at intake by a credentialed adult education instructor, with progress reviewed every eight weeks. GED preparation is introduced at the intermediate level and accelerated for participants who reach benchmark literacy scores, ensuring the most ready learners move toward credentialing within the grant period.

*Component 2: Parent-Child Shared Reading.* Twice monthly, participants attend a 90-minute Family Reading Night, offered in coordination with the Eastside County Public Library. Each session is facilitated by a literacy coach and pairs adult learners with their K–3 children for structured read-aloud activities, followed by brief parent coaching on at-home reading strategies. This component directly addresses the district's finding that 1,200 K–3 students are reading below grade level, recognizing that classroom instruction alone is insufficient without reinforcement at home. Participants receive a take-home book bag at enrollment and replenish their libraries at each Family Reading Night, removing cost as a barrier to daily reading practice.

*Component 3: Employment Readiness Coaching.* In months 10–18, participants who have reached intermediate literacy benchmarks transition into a six-session employment readiness workshop series, covering résumé writing, interview skills, workplace communication, and financial literacy basics. Sessions are delivered in partnership with the Eastside County Workforce Board, which has pledged $20,000 toward this component and will provide direct connections to job placement services for participants who complete GED preparation. This sequencing is intentional: employment content is introduced after participants have built sufficient literacy skills to engage with written materials and self-advocacy tasks, increasing the likelihood that coaching translates into actual job attainment.

**Participant Pathway**

All participants enter through a standardized intake process that includes a literacy assessment (TABE 11/12), goal-setting interview, and eligibility verification. ReadForward's current waitlist of 78 adults will be prioritized for Cohort 1 enrollment, ensuring immediate impact from grant launch. To ensure equitable access, participants may apply for a childcare stipend, disbursed per session attended and administered by the Program Coordinator. Transportation assistance is available through the same fund. Combined, these supports — budgeted at $8,000 across the grant period — directly address the two barriers most frequently cited by adults who leave literacy programs before completion. Participants who miss three consecutive sessions are contacted by the Program Coordinator for a retention check-in; those facing acute barriers are connected to wraparound supports through partner referrals. At program exit, each participant receives a transition plan outlining next steps — GED testing, job placement services, or postsecondary enrollment — with a 90-day follow-up contact to track outcomes.
